title: nimbledocs-customer-escalation-latency-anomaly-heatmap-validation-2024-09
body:
Executive summary:

On 2024-09-16 we received an escalation from NimbleDocs (enterprise customer, Dedicated) reporting intermittent p99 latency spikes in their document-summarization route. The customer observed repeated SLO misses (~3% p99 > 800ms) starting ~2024-09-15 18:30 UTC and asked for immediate investigation.

Impact:
- Affected tenant: NimbleDocs dedicated pool (prod-dedicated-us-west-2-nimbledocs).
- Symptom: p50 ~45ms (unchanged), p95 ~180ms (small bump), p99 spiked to 850-1200ms intermittently for 6 hours on 9/15–9/16.
- Surface impact: user-facing timeouts for some summarization batches; increased error rate in app-level retries.
- Business: customer reported degraded UX for live demo customers and asked for SLA credit decision.

Detection and timeline (UTC):
- 2024-09-15 18:28 — NimbleDocs sends first support ticket referencing slow responses and attached request traces.
- 2024-09-15 18:35 — Monitoring alert: Route latency p99 > 800ms for three consecutive 1m windows. Pager notified on-call.
- 2024-09-15 18:40 — On-call (Priya) begins live triage: gather traces, heatmaps, and scheduling/queueing metrics.
- 2024-09-15 19:10 — Initial mitigation: temporarily raised max_concurrent for route to allow more worker parallelism (short-term uplift). Some reduction in start-queue times but p99 still present.
- 2024-09-15 19:45 — Profiling run (perf + runtime counters) started on a repro harness using NimbleDocs sample prompts.
- 2024-09-15 20:30 — Root cause hypothesis refined after kernel-level traces and batcher logs.
- 2024-09-16 02:00 — Hotfix shipped (PR #987): pin kernel selection to optimized INT8 path for affected model variants + quick patch to batcher flush logic.
- 2024-09-16 03:15 — Observed p99 returned to baseline; customer notified.

Investigation notes (details):
1) Reproduction and profiling approach:
- We reproduced using a dedicated repro harness that replays NimbleDocs traffic distribution (prompt length distribution focused on 256–512 tokens, 75% short requests with small context).
- Collected: serving runtime logs, batcher debug output, per-request timing breakdowns (acquire->prefill->kv-lookup->kernel->emit), perf counters from the GPU node, and heap/threads snapshot from the runtime.
- Also instrumented heatmap-style traces across many requests to correlate queueing delays vs kernel execution time.

2) What we observed:
- Two distinct latency modes: normal (kernel exec ~30–60ms, overall ~40–80ms) and degraded (kernel exec ~400–600ms for a subset of requests).
- Heatmap correlation showed that degraded requests clustered to certain worker instances and correlated with an increase in kernel-launch stalls (observed higher GPU stream synchronization time).
- Batcher logs showed occasional large micro-batches (20–40 tokens combined) for low-concurrency windows caused by an edge-case in the batcher flush timer when bursty short-requests arrive with a slightly higher inter-arrival time distribution.
- Kernel selector logs indicated that for degraded requests the runtime selected the fallback float32 kernel (higher latency) instead of the quantized INT8 path. This selection happened for requests routed to workers that had recently been rebuilt with a new kernel cache invalidation path (deploy from 2024-09-13).
- GPU perf counters pointed at inconsistent memory copy patterns: periods of high H2D memcpy stalls right before kernel dispatch on impacted workers.

3) Root cause (combined):
- Primary: A regression in the post-deployment kernel cache invalidation logic caused some workers to miss the cached INT8 kernels and fall back to float32 kernels for a subset of model shapes. The fallback increased kernel execution time by ~6–8x for those requests.
- Secondary: Under the same traffic pattern, the batcher flush timer edge-case produced uneven micro-batches that increased head-of-line wait for some requests, magnifying the p99 impact.
- Tertiary (contributory): GPU transfer scheduling on the affected hosts showed transient H2D queue bursts due to small, frequent memcpy calls from instrumented telemetry that inadvertently ran in the hot path on the rebuilt workers (added in a debug build during the Sept 13 rolling deploy).

Why this was customer-visible while other tenants were not:
- NimbleDocs has a request distribution that concentrates a higher proportion of short prompts that produce small kernels where the INT8 vs float32 delta is largest.
- Their dedicated pool had a handful of nodes that received the Sept 13 deploy early due to our staged rollout timing.

Mitigations and fixes applied:
- Short-term (within hours):
  - Reverted the kernel-cache invalidation change on the small set of impacted worker instances (rollback + restart).
  - Adjusted batcher flush timeout for the customer's pool to reduce the chance of large micro-batches (route-level override).
  - Disabled in-hotpath telemetry memcpy (moved to async telemetry queue).
  - Communication: Sent status updates to NimbleDocs and offered immediate remediation guidance.

- Hotfix (PR #987):
  - Pin the kernel selector to prefer cached INT8 kernels when available and add defensive rebind logic to rehydrate cache on first miss rather than silently falling back.
  - Add a fast-path that bypasses the debug telemetry memcpy on hot codepath in runtime builds.
  - Add unit and integration tests for batcher flush timer in bursty short-request patterns.

Validation and benchmark results (post-fix):
- Re-run of the repro harness after hotfix and full rollback yielded: p99 reduced from 950ms (median of incidents) to 72ms across 2 hours of mixed traffic. p95 improved from 210ms to 160ms. p50 unchanged.
- Micro-batch distribution returned to expected shape (median batch size 1–3 tokens, occasional larger batches up to 6 under load).
- GPU perf counters: H2D memcpy stalls eliminated on patched workers (measured 0.8% of kernel time vs 9% in degraded mode).

Postmortem analysis (what failed in our systems/process):
- Rollout/testing blind spot: The kernel-cache invalidation change was low-risk and rolled early without an adequate synthetic workload that mimics short-prompt-heavy customers. Our canary criteria did not include short-prompt centric heatmaps.
- Observability gap: We did not have a rule that correlates kernel selector fallbacks with latency alerts; selection logs lived in debug-level logs and were not scraped into aggregated monitoring.
- Release engineering: Staging rollout staged by region + customer affinity caused a small set of dedicated pools to run mixed builds longer than expected.
- Instrumentation: We accidentally included a synchronous telemetry memcpy in the hot path for debug builds which worsened the regression on rebuilt workers.

Action items (owners and ETA):
- Immediate (done): Rollback + hotfix deployment to all dedicated pools (Priya, 9/16).
- Short-term (2 weeks):
  - INF-4321: Add kernel-selector metrics to the global exporter and create alert rule for fallback rate > 0.5% per minute (Miguel, due 2024-09-30).
  - INF-4322: Add synthetic canary tests that include short-prompt-heavy workloads and heatmap correlation validation (Elena, due 2024-10-07).
  - INF-4323: Harden batcher flush timer tests and add fuzzing for inter-arrival timing (Arjun, due 2024-10-05).
- Medium-term (1 quarter):
  - Rework staged rollout to avoid mixing debug builds into dedicated customer pools and add a preflight check that prevents debug telemetry in production builds (Release Eng + Platform, Q4 2024).
  - Performance roadmap item: tighter kernel cache rehydration story with proactive warmup on node start (ServRuntime, Q4 2024).

Customer communications:
- 2024-09-16 04:00 UTC — Sent detailed post-incident note describing root cause and mitigations; offered follow-up technical review and credits per SLA. NimbleDocs accepted the explanation and requested a technical review session with their SREs (scheduled 2024-09-23).

Lessons learned / recommendations:
- Expand canary workload types to cover tail scenarios: short prompts, single-token-heavy workloads, and mixed-length bursts.
- Surface kernel selection behavior into monitoring and build alerting around unexpected fallbacks.
- Limit debug telemetry in the hot path by default and gate any synchronous copying that touches GPU buffers.
- For Dedicated customers, avoid mixing debug builds or staged rollouts that include hot-path instrumentation.

Appendix (notes from profiling):
- Example per-request timing breakdown (degraded request): acquire: 6ms, prefill: 12ms, kv-lookup: 8ms, kernel_launch_and_exec: 540ms, emit: 14ms, total: 580ms.
- Example per-request timing breakdown (normal request): acquire: 4ms, prefill: 10ms, kv-lookup: 6ms, kernel_launch_and_exec: 45ms, emit: 8ms, total: 73ms.
- Kernel-selector trace excerpt (sanitized):
  [2024-09-15T19:12:05Z] model=rw-v2-shard shape=1x256 cache_hit=false -> fallback_kernel=float32
  [2024-09-15T19:12:05Z] model=rw-v2-shard shape=1x256 attempt_rehydrate=true -> rebind_failed

- Relevant PRs/commits: PR #987 (hotfix), earlier deploy PR #963 (Sept 13) contained the cache invalidation changes.

Document history:
- Drafted: Priya Nair (on-call) 2024-09-16
- Profiling and verification: Miguel Santos & Elena Park 2024-09-15 -> 2024-09-16
- Hotfix authored by Arjun Menon 2024-09-16

If there are questions or you want the raw profiling traces/heatmaps, I can upload the pprof/perf tarball and the repro harness logs to the incident folder on Drive and link them here.
